intro: Adlestrop's churchyard yew went unrecorded until 2012, when Lin Carter found it and the Ancient Yew Group came to measure. It turned out to be 6.33 metres round near the ground, a male yew in two trunks joined low down, by the west wall of St Mary Magdalene's churchyard. Someone has fitted a curved seat round its south side. The churchyard is open and free, in a small village a few kilometres from Moreton-in-Marsh.
meta_description: Nobody recorded the Adlestrop churchyard yew until 2012. It is 6.33 metres round near the ground, likely over 500 years old, and stands by the west wall.
question_meta: Adlestrop's oldest tree is a churchyard yew 6.33 metres round, first recorded in 2012 and likely over 500 years old by the Ancient Yew Group's girth bands.
question_answer: The oldest tree in Adlestrop is the yew in St Mary Magdalene's churchyard, 6.33 metres round near the ground. The Ancient Yew Group classes a yew this size as ancient, likely over 500 years old. That is an estimate from girth, not a dating, and the tree was only recorded in 2012.
question_context: For a tree of its size, the Adlestrop yew kept a remarkably low profile. It does not appear in the Ancient Yew Group's register until 2012, when Lin Carter came across it. Tim Hills then recorded a male yew of two trunks joined near the ground, the larger fragment about 14 feet round and the smaller about 10, both covered in ivy, with a combined girth of 20 feet 9 inches, or 633 centimetres, taken just above the ground. Peter Norton's 2017 visit repeated the figure. Hills judged that the two trunks look like sections of a once larger tree. Because the measurement is taken round both trunks at the base, it reads larger than a normal chest-height girth would. On the Group's banding, which puts yews of five to seven metres in its ancient class, the likely age is over 500 years. Nobody has dated it. The church beside it has a 14th or 15th century tower, and the rest of the building was rebuilt between 1750 and 1764.

faq.q: Where is the yew in Adlestrop churchyard?
faq.a: Close to the west wall of the churchyard, west of the tower, with a curved seat round its south and south-east side and a stone lean-to shed beside it.

faq.q: How do I get to Adlestrop?
faq.a: Moreton-in-Marsh is the nearest mainline station, roughly 6 km away. From there a car or taxi is the practical way.

trees.name: The Adlestrop churchyard yew

location.address: St Mary Magdalene churchyard, Adlestrop, Gloucestershire GL56 0YN

trees.story:
Until 2012 nobody had written this yew down. It had stood by the west wall of this Cotswold churchyard for centuries, and the Ancient Yew Group only added it to their register after Lin Carter found it that year. Then Tim Hills came to measure, and the tape went round to 6.33 metres, taken near the ground where the two trunks meet.

Two trunks, because this is a split tree. It is a male yew in two fragments joined low down, the larger about 14 feet round and the smaller about 10, both heavily wrapped in ivy. Hills thought they looked like sections of one once larger tree. The girth is measured around both together at the base, so it reads bigger than a chest-height figure would.

The Ancient Yew Group's girth bands put a yew of this size in the ancient class, likely over 500 years. That is an estimate from size, not a dating, but on it the yew is older than most of St Mary Magdalene's church, whose tower is 14th or 15th century and whose body was rebuilt between 1750 and 1764.

Someone has put a curved seat round its south side. It is the right instinct. This is a tree for sitting next to, slowly.

trees.access: Open churchyard (Ancient Yew Group lists access as public; church parochial church council ground). Free, no opening hours.
trees.transport: Adlestrop village near Moreton-in-Marsh (nearest mainline station, roughly 6 km); car or taxi.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the two ivy-covered trunks joined near the ground, with a curved seat round the south side. It stands by the west wall of the churchyard, west of the tower, beside a stone lean-to shed.
trees.verify_notes: AYG: ancient yew unrecorded until Lin Carter found it in 2012; Tim Hills recorded a male yew of two trunks joined near the ground, girth 20 ft 9 in (633 cm at 5 cm; 2012, Hills; repeated 2017 Norton), larger fragment 14 ft 1 in, smaller 10 ft 4 in, ivy-covered. Hills judges the two trunks look like sections of a once larger tree. AYG classifies girth 5-7 m as ancient, likely age above 500 years (AYG's own banding: derived age, broad). Site file dated 2024 and girth grid 2017 give recent revisits (alive). Church: tower 14th/15th century, rest 1750-1764. Source: AYG only (specialist register, three separate recorders), flagged 'one source'. Ground held by the Parochial Church Council; open churchyard. Position AYG grid SP24302690 converted; approximate. Girth is the whole-tree girth near the ground at 5 cm, so it overstates a normal 1.5 m girth: state as 'near the ground'.
